We focus on founder-owned staffing, consulting, accounting, MSP, agency, training, and subscription-based service businesses with $5M–$50M in annual revenue and $1M–$5M+ in EBITDA. These firms are large enough to attract strategic consolidators, professional-services PE, and family-office capital, but still benefit from the personalized attention of a boutique M&A advisory firm. What business services sub-sectors do you advise? Staffing and recruiting, B2B consulting and boutique advisory, accounting and bookkeeping, IT managed services, digital marketing and creative agencies, B2B training and education, and subscription-based B2B services. Each sub-sector has its own buyer pool, its own value drivers, and its own multiple range, and we calibrate the process accordingly. My firm is a personal-services business where I'm the rainmaker. Is it sellable? Often yes, but the work has to start two to three years ahead of going to market. The most common reason a services firm fails to sell is founder dependency: clients stay because of the founder's relationship, sales come from the founder's calendar, and key processes live in the founder's head. Pre-sale advisory work focuses on reducing each of those dependencies: distributing client relationships, productizing acquisition, and documenting process, so the firm becomes tradeable. We've seen the difference between a $5M services firm that sells at 4x and one that sells at 7x come down to exactly this. Will my customers, team, or competitors find out we're exploring a sale? No. Confidentiality is built into the process from day one. No public listing on any marketplace. Buyer outreach is direct and targeted, with no firm name, client list, or financials shared before an NDA is signed. We focus on founder-owned staffing, consulting, accounting, MSP, agency, training, and subscription-based service businesses with $5M–$50M in annual revenue and $1M–$5M+ in EBITDA. These firms are large enough to attract strategic consolidators, professional-services PE, and family-office capital, but still benefit from the personalized attention of a boutique M&A advisory firm. What business services sub-sectors do you advise? Staffing and recruiting, B2B consulting and boutique advisory, accounting and bookkeeping, IT managed services, digital marketing and creative agencies, B2B training and education, and subscription-based B2B services. Each sub-sector has its own buyer pool, its own value drivers, and its own multiple range, and we calibrate the process accordingly. My firm is a personal-services business where I'm the rainmaker. Is it sellable? Often yes, but the work has to start two to three years ahead of going to market. The most common reason a services firm fails to sell is founder dependency: clients stay because of the founder's relationship, sales come from the founder's calendar, and key processes live in the founder's head. Pre-sale advisory work focuses on reducing each of those dependencies: distributing client relationships, productizing acquisition, and documenting process, so the firm becomes tradeable. title: Sell Your Companyfor What It'sActually Worth
description: Common Questions Questions Owners Ask Us Straight answers to what sellers want to know before they ever pick up the phone. What size companies does Valorem Advisors work with? We focus on founder-owned and family-owned companies generating roughly $5M to $50M in annual revenue, or $1M+ in EBITDA. Smaller Main Street businesses are served through Valorem Business Brokers. How is M&A advisory different from listing my business with a broker? A broker lists and waits. We run a confidential, competitive process: institutional valuation, targeted outreach to qualified strategic and financial buyers, and managed bidding designed to create tension and drive enterprise value. The goal is a premium outcome, not a quick sale. Will my employees, customers, or competitors find out my company is for sale? No. Every buyer interaction is gated behind a structured NDA process. We never contact your employees, customers, or competitors without your explicit permission, and your identity stays protected until you choose to reveal it. What is my business worth? Lower middle market companies are typically valued on a multiple of EBITDA or SDE, adjusted for growth, customer concentration, management depth, and recurring revenue. We provide a confidential Broker Opinion of Value so you know your number before you decide anything. How long does it take to sell a lower middle market company? A typical sell-side process runs six to twelve months from engagement to close, depending on financial readiness, the buyer universe, and diligence. Owners who prepare 12–36 months ahead usually sell faster and for more. When should I start the conversation if I want to sell in a few years? Sooner than you think. The owners who capture the highest values start 12 to 36 months out, giving us time to close value gaps, reduce key-person risk, and clean up financials before going to market. title: Confidential Business BrokerageforOwner-Operators
description: Frequently Asked Common Questions from Main Street Owners What size businesses does Valorem Business Brokers represent? Our brokerage practice focuses on owner-operated South Florida service businesses with sale prices from $250,000 to $5 million, typically generating $100,000 to $1 million in Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE). For businesses with $5M+ in revenue and $1M+ in EBITDA, we run a separate lower middle market M&A advisory process under our Valorem Advisors practice . How long does it take to sell a Main Street business? From engagement to closing, a well-prepared business with clean books typically takes 6 to 12 months. The valuation and CIM build takes 2 to 4 weeks, marketing and buyer screening runs 60 to 120 days, due diligence and SBA underwriting adds another 60 to 90 days, and closing closes out the timeline. Businesses with messy financials, customer concentration, or heavy owner dependency take longer or sometimes don't sell at all without preparation work upfront. What is my business worth? Main Street businesses are most commonly valued as a multiple of Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE) — typically 2.0x to 3.5x, depending on vertical, recurring revenue, customer concentration, owner separability, and growth runway. We start every engagement with a no-cost Broker's Opinion of Value (BOV) that establishes a defensible range using your last three years of financials, comparable closed transactions in your vertical, and current SBA-financed buyer activity. Understanding the process can help ensure that you are able to qualify for the home loan that you need. Lenders look at two things when determining if you are able to qualify for a home loan: your ability to repay the loan and your willingness to repay it. Ability to repay The first thing that a lender wants to know is if you are able to repay the loan for which you are applying. The lender looks at your current employment. Have you been in the same job for at least two years or at least the same line of work for a few years? This shows the lender that you have steady employment, and its a great plus in qualifying for a home loan. The lender also looks at your total income and compares it to your debts, adding in your proposed monthly mortgage payment. You must have sufficient income to comfortably make these payments. This reflects your ability to repay the loan when qualifying for a home loan. If the lender believes your debt load is too high, you will qualify for a smaller loan and likely be charged a higher interest rate. Therefore, it makes sense to pay off as much debt as possible before applying for a home loan. Willingness to repay The next step in qualifying for a home loan is determining your willingness to repay the loan. Lenders determine this by looking at how you have paid off debt in the past, and it is one reason why lenders check your credit report. If you have faithfully made on-time payments toward your past debts, it helps you when qualifying for a home loan. The lender also looks at how you intend to use the property that you are buying. Offers 5BR + gym (can be converted to 6th BR) 7+2BA, and approximately 13,500 SF (per owner) across three levels, featuring soaring 24’+ ceilings, marble floors, and walls of glass framing breathtaking bay views. Expansive living, dining, and kitchen areas open to large terraces, creating seamless indoor-outdoor living ideal for both everyday comfort and grand-scale entertaining. Resort-style grounds include a piano-shaped saltwater pool, cabana bath, lush tropical landscaping, and expansive lawn areas with artfully integrated lighting extending the estate’s experience well beyond sunset. A private marina, formerly a presidential helipad—features rare 3-phase power and dockage for yachts up to 200’, plus over 34,000 SF of submerged land, making this one of Miami’s most significant and irreplaceable waterfront holdings in the world.

Additional en-suite bedrooms offer generous accommodations for guests. The second floor also includes two laundry rooms, a lounge/additional guest suite, and multiple balconies overlooking the water and grounds.  The lower level is designed for both function and recreation, with ample storage, a large exercise room, spa bath and sauna, memorabilia room, and expansive 18+/- car garage ideal for the avid collector. Beautifully landscaped and impeccably maintained grounds stretch from the Ocean to the Intracoastal. Multiple terraces and covered loggias surround the 53-foot infinity swimming pool with sun shelf, creating exceptional spaces for outdoor entertaining and relaxation. Business Overview Request NDA/Cim BUYER SHOULD HAVE EXTENSIVE METAL FABRICATION KNOWLEDGE AND EXPERIENCE. 

No sales team. No marketing. No second shift. No website worth mentioning. And yet — $5.75 million in revenue last year. $4.89M the year before. $4.38M the year before that. Three years of growth without lifting a finger to sell.

You want to know why? Because this shop fabricates precision sheet metal for Google, Nike, the MTA, Macy's, Bloomingdale's, Sephora, Lululemon, Hudson Yard, and JCDecaux — and when you do the work right for clients like that, you don't need to advertise. The referrals never stop.

description: COMMON QUESTIONS Your questions, answered directly. If something is unclear after reading through these, the next step is a conversation. We want to understand where your practice is before recommending anything. START A CONVERSATION Do I have to take everything, or can I start with one piece? You start with either the website or the CRM. Deal management is its own software, tied to the CRM, so it arrives with the CRM rather than being a separate starting point. Whichever you begin with is built to connect to the rest, so adding the next piece later is an extension rather than a rebuild. Who designs and builds the website? The Deal Studio design team. It starts with a Brand Sprint to settle your positioning and messaging, then we handle the design, the build, the hosting, and the ongoing updates, and we wire it into your CRM as part of the build rather than afterward. What is a Brand Sprint? A focused working session before design starts. We work through who you serve, what you want to be known for, and how you talk about it, and the site gets built from what comes out of it. Its job is a website that says something specific about you from the day it launches rather than something generic. It is deliberately narrow: the Sprint settles the site, and it does not produce a brand guide. How is that different from a full brand engagement? Depth, and what comes out the other side. The Sprint settles positioning and messaging so the website can launch as something specific to you. A full brand engagement goes further: research into your market and the people you are trying to reach, positioning developed from the ground up, and a brand system built around connected outcomes, where one guide goes on to produce campaigns, content, resources, and new opportunities rather than a single website. title: What Buyers Really Want From a Business Sale
description: Seller Articles What Buyers Really Want From a Business Sale September 25, 2026 When you’re selling a business, it’s natural to focus on the number you want to receive. But experienced sellers know that a successful transaction involves much more than agreeing on a price. The amount of cash changing hands, the financing structure, the buyer’s ability to operate the business, and the expectations of both parties can all influence whether a deal actually comes together. The key is finding a structure that makes sense for both sides. A buyer may be willing to pay a strong price for a good business, but the amount of cash required upfront can have a significant impact on whether the transaction is workable. Seller financing can sometimes bridge that gap. Rather than requiring the buyer to provide the entire purchase price in cash at closing, a seller may finance a portion of the purchase. This can make the business accessible to a larger pool of qualified buyers while giving the seller the opportunity to receive payments over time. For buyers, the question is often simple: Can this business support the purchase price and provide enough income to make the investment worthwhile? For sellers, there’s a similar question: Can I structure the transaction in a way that gives the buyer a realistic chance to succeed while still achieving my financial goals? The best deal structure considers both. Qualified Buyers Matter Not every person who expresses interest in buying a business is ready or able to complete a transaction. A serious buyer should have a realistic understanding of the financial commitment involved, the responsibilities of ownership, and what it will take to operate the company successfully. This is one reason buyer qualification is such an important part of the selling process. A seller doesn’t simply need someone who likes the business. title: What Buyers Really Want From a Business Sale - Foresight Business Brokers
description: When you’re selling a business, it’s natural to focus on the number you want to receive. But experienced sellers know that a successful transaction involves much more than agreeing on a price. The amount of cash changing hands, the financing structure, the buyer’s ability to operate the business, and the expectations of both parties can all influence whether a deal actually comes together. The key is finding a structure that makes sense for both sides. A buyer may be willing to pay a strong price for a good business, but the amount of cash required upfront can have a significant impact on whether the transaction is workable. Seller financing can sometimes bridge that gap. Rather than requiring the buyer to provide the entire purchase price in cash at closing, a seller may finance a portion of the purchase. This can make the business accessible to a larger pool of qualified buyers while giving the seller the opportunity to receive payments over time. For buyers, the question is often simple: Can this business support the purchase price and provide enough income to make the investment worthwhile? For sellers, there’s a similar question: Can I structure the transaction in a way that gives the buyer a realistic chance to succeed while still achieving my financial goals? The best deal structure considers both. Qualified Buyers Matter Not every person who expresses interest in buying a business is ready or able to complete a transaction. A serious buyer should have a realistic understanding of the financial commitment involved, the responsibilities of ownership, and what it will take to operate the company successfully. This is one reason buyer qualification is such an important part of the selling process. A seller doesn’t simply need someone who likes the business. They need a buyer who has the financial resources, motivation, and ability to move forward. A qualified buyer also gives the seller greater confidence when considering terms such as seller financing. description: Seller Articles Does Your Asking Price Help or Hurt Your Business Sale? by Deal Studio on September 18, 2026 One of the most important decisions a business owner makes when preparing to sell is determining the right asking price. It is natural to want the highest possible value for a company built through years of hard work, sacrifice, and dedication. However, the market ultimately determines what a business is worth. Setting an asking price based on the company’s financial performance, strengths, and current market conditions is one of the best ways to attract qualified buyers. Some sellers take the approach of starting with a higher asking price and lowering it later if necessary. While this may seem like a reasonable strategy, it can create challenges. Buyers often use the asking price as their first indication of whether a business is a realistic opportunity. If the price does not align with the company’s earnings, assets, and market value, many qualified buyers may never take the time to explore further. An overpriced business can also spend more time on the market, causing buyers to question why it has not sold. A realistic asking price, on the other hand, can create more interest, encourage serious conversations, and lead to stronger negotiations. Determining the right price requires looking beyond what an owner hopes to receive. Buyers evaluate factors such as profitability, revenue trends, customer relationships, growth opportunities, operational systems, and risk. Two businesses in the same industry can have very different values depending on how they perform and how well they are positioned for future success. A business broker can provide valuable perspective throughout this process. title: What Makes a Business Attractive to Buyers? - Foresight Business Brokers
description: Seller Articles What Makes a Business Attractive to Buyers? by Deal Studio on September 11, 2026 Many business owners wonder whether their industry will determine how easy it is to sell their business. While certain industries may experience periods of higher demand than others, buyers rarely make decisions based on industry alone. More often, they focus on the quality of the business itself. A well-managed company with strong financial performance will generally attract more interest than a struggling business in a “hot” industry. Understanding what buyers value can help owners make improvements long before they decide to sell. Buyers Look Beyond the Industry Every buyer has unique goals. Some are looking to expand an existing business, while others want to become business owners for the first time. Investment groups may be searching for companies with strong cash flow, while strategic buyers may value opportunities to grow through acquisition. Despite these different motivations, most buyers evaluate businesses using many of the same criteria. They want confidence that the business can continue to succeed after the ownership transition. Consistent profitability is often at the top of the list. Buyers also appreciate reliable cash flow, accurate financial records, and a business that has demonstrated stable performance over time. These factors help reduce uncertainty and make it easier for buyers and lenders to evaluate the opportunity. description:
About us We provide business broker and advisory services to small to mid-size Pacific Northwest businesses.  Businesses we proudly represent have revenue of $2M - $30M and span industry verticals.      

The Pacific Northwest is our home. It’s a thriving, growing hub that has long attracted business owners and innovators from across the United States and, increasingly, the world. It is known for Amazon, Starbucks, Microsoft, Boeing, Nike, T-Mobile – the list goes on. Thriving and growing along with these firms and our burgeoning population are 609,000+ Washington businesses and an additional 368,000 in Oregon.

We do not sell you on selling your business or buying one. Instead we will listen, provide options and expertise, and ultimately partner with you to accomplish your goals.

Put our experts to work for you in valuing, optimizing a business for sale, identifying and qualifying buyers, negotiating, deal structuring, and closing. Register Here Get in Touch (206) 703-3555 info@wabusinessbrokers.com Seattle, WA 98199 Expert Business Valuations Understanding the worth of your business is just as important as knowing your personal credit score or having a will drawn up. It offers numerous benefits, including comparing its current value to the previous year, identifying strengths and areas for improvement, calculating revenue per employee, qualifying for bank loans or financing, planning for the future and retirement, and creating a succession plan. Imagine someone approaching you with an offer to buy your business – wouldn’t you want to know if the price is fair or even too good to refuse? Getting a professional valuation of your business is one of the wisest investments any owner can make. Valuations serve various purposes like in divorce proceedings, for bank loans, employee stock option purchases, or liquidation. However, if you’re looking to know the fair market value for selling your business, we offer low-priced valuations. In fact, for every business we list for sale, we generate a Valuation Report before putting it on the market. This benefits both the seller, as it provides insights into the business’s value, and the buyer, as it helps them understand the reasons behind the asking price, making the entire process more transparent and reasonable. title: Why Every Business Owner Should Always Be Prepared to Sell
description: Blog Home / Selling Business Selling Business Why Every Business Owner Should Always Be Prepared to Sell Posted by Tony Moon January 20, 2026 On December 23, 2025 Why Every Business Owner Should Always be Prepared to Sell Many business owners don’t plan to sell their business suddenly. Sometimes, the decision is triggered by life such as health issues, family changes, partnership challenges, or an unexpected opportunity. The problem is that many owners are forced to sell before their business is ready, which often leads to lower value, tougher negotiations, and fewer qualified buyers. At Peak Biz Brokers & Advisors, we believe every business owner should always be prepared to sell even if selling isn’t currently part of the plan. Preparation creates options, protects value, and keeps control in the owner’s hands. Selling a Business Is More Complex Than Most Owners Expect A business may appear successful on the surface, but buyers and lenders evaluate businesses very differently than owners do. Buyers typically want to know: Is cash flow consistent, documented, and sustainable? Can the business operate without the owner’s daily involvement? Are systems, processes, and contracts transferable? Will the business support debt while still generating income? If these questions aren’t clearly answered, buyers perceive risk and risk directly impacts valuation, deal structure, and buyer interest. Being Prepared to Sell Doesn't Mean You're Ready to Exit One of the most common misconceptions is that sale preparation only matters when an owner is ready to sell. In reality, preparing a business for sale improves the business today, not just at exit. A sale-ready business typically has: Clean, well-organized financial statements Efficient operations and documented procedures Reduced reliance on the owner Transferable customer and vendor relationships Predictable and defensible cash flow These characteristics make a business more valuable whether it’s sold or not.
